**Who this is for.** You know rigid-body dynamics and Coulomb friction, but
not how a certificate turns "which forces act at the contacts?" into a
computation it can prove things about. This page derives that computation
from first principles, with a worked example you can check by hand. The
manipulated object is the **block**; a **box** on this page is only a
product of intervals, as in [interval arithmetic](interval-arithmetic.qmd).
Companions: [deciding support](support-tutorial.qmd) (the static question),
[certified funnels and composition](funnel-composition.qmd) and [the
techniques that made the chain certify](certification-techniques.qmd). The
code is `endpoint_generic.Edge.contact_data` and
`post_impact_rest.class_maps` on branch `exp/edge-endpoints`; the technical
report's Chapter 19 has the same material with proofs.

## 1. The question at an instant

**Intuition.** The [deciding-support page](support-tutorial.qmd) asks a
static question: *can* some contact forces hold the block? A moving block
asks a sharper one. At this instant, with these positions, velocities and
motor force, which contact forces *does* rigid-body mechanics with Coulomb
friction produce, and what accelerations follow? Does a contact open, stick,
or slide, and which way? A certificate needs the answer not at one state but
at every state of a box, and it needs to know that the answer the plan
relies on is the *only* one.

**The plan of the page.** Equations of motion (§2), each contact as two rows
of a Jacobian (§3), the Delassus form (§4), classes and the class solve
(§5), why the landing's flat family has no velocity terms (§6), the
enclosure over a box (§7), excluding and certifying classes (§8), and what
an independent check of the code found (§9).

## 2. Two bodies, five coordinates

**The convention.** The plane is $x$–$z$, $z$ up. The $y$ axis points into
the page, and the block's tilt $\theta$ is a rotation about it, so a
body-fixed vector $b$ has world components
$$
R(\theta)\,b = (b_x\cos\theta + b_z\sin\theta,\; -b_x\sin\theta + b_z\cos\theta).
$$
Differentiating, a body-fixed vector with world components $r$ turns at
$$
\dot r = \dot\theta\,\rho(r), \qquad \rho(r) = (r_z,\,-r_x).
$$
$\rho$ is a quarter turn, so $\rho(\rho(r)) = -r$ and
$a\cdot\rho(b) = -\rho(a)\cdot b$.

**Coordinates and masses.** $q = (x_B, z_B, \theta, x_M, z_M)$: the block's
centre $c$, its tilt, and the disk's centre $P_M$. The disk is the robot's
end effector: it translates and does not spin. With $u$ the motor force on
the disk,
$$
M = \operatorname{diag}(m_B, m_B, I_B, m_M, m_M), \qquad
f = (0,\,-m_B g,\,0,\,u_x,\,u_z - m_M g).
$$
The scene: $m_B = 0.1$ kg, side $a = 125$ mm, $I_B = m_B a^2/6$,
$m_M = 0.02$ kg, disk radius $15.625$ mm, environment friction $0.2$, disk
friction anywhere in $[0.3, 0.5]$.

**A material point.** The block's point at world offset $r$ from the centre
moves at
$$
\dot p = \dot c + \dot\theta\,\rho(r) = (\dot x_B + \dot\theta r_z,\; \dot z_B - \dot\theta r_x).
$$

## 3. A contact is two rows

**Intuition.** Each contact has a normal $n$ and a tangent $t$. What matters
is how fast the gap closes ($v_n$) and how fast the surfaces slip ($v_t$).
Both are linear in the velocities, so each is a row of a Jacobian.

**Block on a fixed environment** ($n$ into the block):
$$
v_e = e\cdot\dot p, \qquad J_e = (e_x,\; e_z,\; e_x r_z - e_z r_x,\; 0,\; 0), \qquad e\in\{n,t\}.
$$
**The disk on a block face** ($n$ the face's outward normal, $K = P_M - Rn$
the block's point under the disk, $r = K - c$; the disk relative to the
block):
$$
J_e = (-e_x,\; -e_z,\; -(e_x r_z - e_z r_x),\; e_x,\; e_z).
$$
**Forces come through the transpose.** A contact force
$\lambda_n n + \lambda_t t$ does work $\lambda_n v_n + \lambda_t v_t$, so its
generalized force is $J^\top\lambda$. The third entry of a row is the torque
arm; the disk's row applies $+\lambda$ to the disk and $-\lambda$ to the
block. Action and reaction come out of the rows.

**Check it by hand.** A unit force straight up ($e = (0,1)$) at the block's
bottom corner on its $+x$ side, $r = (a/2, -a/2)$ at $\theta = 0$: the row is
$(0, 1, -a/2, 0, 0)$, a torque of $-a/2$ about $y$. Drawn with $+x$ to the
right and $y$ into the page, a positive $\theta$ turns the block clockwise;
a push up on the right side turns it counterclockwise, a negative
$\theta$, as the sign says.

**The sign of a slip matters.** A class below says "slides with $v_t > 0$",
so the tangent's direction is part of the model. After the landing the disk
presses on the block's left face, whose tangent in the code is
$t_D = (0,-1)$: $v_t > 0$ means the disk moves *down* the face relative to
the block.

## 4. The Delassus form

**Derivation.** Stack the closed contacts' rows into $J$ and their forces
into $\lambda$. Newton–Euler is
$$
M\ddot q = f + J^\top \lambda .
$$
The contact accelerations are $a = J\ddot q + \dot J\dot q$. Substitute
$\ddot q$:
$$
\boxed{\; a = W\lambda + a_f, \qquad W = J M^{-1} J^\top, \qquad a_f = J M^{-1} f + \dot J\dot q \;}
$$
$W$, the **Delassus matrix**, says how hard each contact force pushes each
contact's acceleration: symmetric, positive semidefinite, definite when the
rows are independent. $a_f$ is what the contacts would do with no contact
force at all: gravity, the motor, and the velocity terms $\dot J\dot q$.
Signorini's condition ($0 \le \lambda_n \perp a_n \ge 0$) and Coulomb's law
close the system. That is the contact problem of Moreau
[@moreau1988unilateral] and of the textbooks
[@pfeiffer1996multibody; @brogliato2016nonsmooth], a linear complementarity
problem (LCP) in $\lambda$ [@pang1996complementarity]; its velocity-level
version is the time step of Stewart and Trinkle [@stewart1996implicit] and
Anitescu and Potra [@anitescu1997formulating]. It can have no solution or
several, so a certificate does not assume either away. It enumerates.

**Check it by hand.** After the landing the block rests on the platform and
cannot turn (§6). Lump the platform's two supports into one contact $t$
(normal $(0,1)$, tangent $(1,0)$) and keep the disk $D$ on the left face
(normal $(-1,0)$, tangent $(0,-1)$). Then
$M^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(10,10,50,50)$ on $(x_B, z_B, x_M, z_M)$, the
rows are $(0,1,0,0)$, $(1,0,0,0)$, $(1,0,-1,0)$, $(0,1,0,-1)$, and with the
hold force $u = (0.1,\, m_M g)$ N:
$$
W = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 0 & 0 & 10\\ 0 & 10 & 10 & 0\\ 0 & 10 & 60 & 0\\ 10 & 0 & 0 & 60\end{pmatrix},\qquad
a_f = \begin{pmatrix} -9.804\\ 0\\ -5\\ -9.804 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{m/s}^2 .
$$
One newton on the platform's normal lifts the block at $1/m_B = 10$ m/s²; one
newton between disk and block separates them at $1/m_B + 1/m_M = 60$ m/s².
With no contact forces the block falls at $g$ and the disk runs into it at
$0.1/m_M = 5$ m/s² (negative means closing).

![The flat family after the landing (+x to the left, as in the paper). The block slides forward on the platform's corner e₀ and on its own corner b₁; the disk presses on the block's face under the hold force u and slips up the face. Every contact frame is horizontal or vertical, and the block does not turn.](media/bg_class_solve_flat.svg){.lightbox}

## 5. Classes: guess, solve, check

**Intuition.** Coulomb's law is a switch: a contact is open, sticks, or
slides one way or the other. Guess the switch position at every contact.
Each guess, a **class**, makes the problem linear and square. Solve it, then
check whether the guess was consistent.

::: {.table-responsive}

| Class | Meaning | Equations | Conditions (from $v_t = 0$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| O | open | $\lambda_n = 0,\ \lambda_t = 0$ | $a_n > 0$ |
| S | sticks | $a_n = 0,\ a_t = 0$ | $\lambda_n \ge 0,\ \lvert\lambda_t\rvert \le \mu\lambda_n$ |
| P | slides, $v_t > 0$ | $a_n = 0,\ \lambda_t + \mu\lambda_n = 0$ | $\lambda_n \ge 0,\ a_t > 0$ |
| N | slides, $v_t < 0$ | $a_n = 0,\ \lambda_t - \mu\lambda_n = 0$ | $\lambda_n \ge 0,\ a_t < 0$ |

:::

With $a = W\lambda + a_f$ substituted, a class is a square system
$A\lambda = b$: a closed contact contributes its row of $W$; a sticking one
its tangential row too; a sliding one the friction law. The code solves it
by Gauss–Jordan elimination in plain scalar operations, so that interval
arithmetic can run through the same code (§7).

**Check it by hand: the block slides forward and the disk slides up the
face.** Up the face is $v_t < 0$ along $t_D$, so the class is (P, N). The
four equations are $a_{n,t} = 0$, $\lambda_{t,t} = -0.2\,\lambda_{n,t}$,
$a_{n,D} = 0$, $\lambda_{t,D} = \mu\lambda_{n,D}$. At $\mu = 0.4$:
$$
\lambda = (0.9346,\ -0.1869,\ 0.1145,\ 0.0458)\ \text{N},\qquad
a = (0,\ -0.7243,\ 0,\ 2.2897)\ \text{m/s}^2 .
$$
The block's horizontal balance: $0.1145 - 0.1869 = 0.1\times(-0.7243)$. The
disk's friction, $0.0458$ N, pushes the disk down and the block up, so the
platform carries only $0.9804 - 0.0458 = 0.9346$ N. Both slips decelerate:
the block at $0.724$ m/s², the disk's upward slip at $2.29$ m/s².

**The other directions.** With the disk sliding *down* (P) its friction
presses the block onto the platform (1.0274 N), and the block decelerates
faster, at $0.879$ m/s². With the disk sticking (S), $\lambda_{t,D} = 0$, the
block decelerates at $0.8007$ m/s², and the cone condition
$0 \le 0.4\times 0.1160$ holds. The slip direction changes the answer by
20%: it is part of the model, not a detail.

**An excluded class: (O, S).** Suppose the block leaves the platform while
the disk sticks. Then $\lambda_{n,D} = 0.0833$ N and
$\lambda_{t,D} = 0.1634$ N. Two conditions fail: the block's normal
acceleration $-8.17$ m/s² is not positive (it would have to sink into the
platform to leave it), and $0.1634 > 0.4\times0.0833$ puts the disk's force
outside its cone. One failure is enough.

## 6. Why the flat family has no velocity terms

**Intuition.** Velocity terms come from turning: a turning body's points
have centripetal accelerations, and its contact frames turn with it. A block
that does not turn has none.

**The derivation.** By hand, with $\omega = \dot\theta$:

- a block point in a fixed frame: $\dot J_e\dot q = -\omega^2\, e\cdot r$;
- the disk's normal row: $2\omega\,\rho(n)\cdot(\dot P_M - \dot c) - \omega^2\, n\cdot(P_M - c)$;
- the disk's tangential row: $2\omega\,\rho(t)\cdot(\dot P_M - \dot c) - \omega^2\, t\cdot(K - c)$.

Every term carries $\omega$. After the landing, the block's two supports on
the platform both have closed normal rows,
$\dot z_B - \omega r_{x,1} = 0$ and $\dot z_B - \omega r_{x,2} = 0$ with
different moment arms, so $\omega = 0$: the **flat family**. There
$a_f = J M^{-1} f$ exactly, whatever the block's speed and the disk's slip.
The accelerations depend on the velocities only through the class (the
friction directions), which is why the rest certificate can evaluate each
class once and use it at every speed.

**One more fact the check confirms.** On the flat family the block only
translates, so its translational equations see only the *sums* of the two
supports' forces. The slips' accelerations therefore do not depend on the
block's position or the disk's place on the face at all (only on the small
tilt offset and on $\mu$); the moment balance only splits the platform's
force between the two supports.

## 7. From a point to a box: the mean-value form

**Intuition.** A certificate needs $\lambda$ and $a$ at every state of a box
$X$ of positions, offsets and friction coefficients. Treat the class
solution as a smooth map $F$ of the state, and bound it by its value at the
box's centre plus the most its slope can add.

**The general statement.** With $m$ the box's centre, $r$ its radius and
$[J]$ an interval enclosure of $F$'s Jacobian over $X$ (immrax's natural
inclusion [@harapanahalli2024immrax]),
$$
F(X) \subseteq F(m) \pm \operatorname{mag}([J])\, r .
$$
*Why it is sound.* For a point $x\in X$ and an output $i$, the mean value
theorem on the segment from $m$ to $x$ gives
$F_i(x) - F_i(m) = \nabla F_i(\xi)\cdot(x - m)$ for some $\xi$ on the segment.
The box is convex, so $\xi \in X$ and $\nabla F_i(\xi)\in [J]_i$; with
$|x - m| \le r$ the bound follows [@moore2009introduction; @neumaier1990interval].

*Why $F$ is smooth there.* $F$ is rational; it can only break where an
elimination pivot vanishes. Every pivot is a divisor in $F$ and its
derivatives, interval division by an interval containing 0 is unbounded, and
the pivot's interval contains its range over $X$. So a *finite* $[J]$
certifies that no pivot vanishes on $X$. A non-finite one leaves the class
undecided, never passed.

**Check it by hand.** In the class (P, N) of §5 the block's acceleration is a
function of $\mu$ alone,
$$
a_t(\mu) = -1.9608 + 69.608\,\frac{1 + 0.2\mu}{60 + 2\mu},
$$
with slope
$696.08/(60 + 2\mu)^2$. Over $\mu\in[0.3,0.5]$: $m = 0.4$, $r = 0.1$,
$a_t(0.4) = -0.72434$, and the slope's interval is
$696.08/[60.6, 61]^2 = [0.18707, 0.18955]$. The enclosure is
$$
-0.72434 \pm 0.018955 = [-0.74330, -0.70539]\ \text{m/s}^2,
$$
against the true range
$[-0.74323, -0.70557]$.

**Where it loses.** Over a large box the Jacobian's natural inclusion
suffers the [dependency effect](interval-arithmetic.qmd): the same entries
of $W$ appear many times in the elimination. On the flat family the slips'
accelerations do not depend on position at all (§6), so any width their
enclosures gain along the position coordinates is pure overestimate. That
is what refuses some boxes after they are grown by the stopping distance,
and splitting the box recovers them.

## 8. Excluding and certifying classes

**Excluding.** A class is excluded on a box when one of its conditions fails
for *every* member, and the enclosure decides that soundly: if the upper end
of $\lambda_n$'s enclosure is negative, no member has $\lambda_n \ge 0$. The
conditions are positive normal forces, the friction cone at sticking
contacts, and the strict sign conditions ($a_n > 0$ to open, $a_t$ in the
direction of a slip that starts from rest).

**Certifying.** The class the plan follows must hold with margin: normal
forces at least the derived floor $N_{\min}$, and every sliding contact
decelerating, $a_t + w \le -a_{\min} < 0$ over the box, with $w$ the
measured residual. Then the slip reaches zero within
$T \le v_t(0)/a_{\min}$ after at most $v_t(0)^2/(2a_{\min})$ of travel, and the
conditions are checked on the box grown by that distance. At zero slip the
class that would restart the slide needs $a_t \ge 0$, which the same
deceleration bound excludes.

**Starting versus moving.** The table's last column is for a contact that
*starts* to slide from $v_t = 0$: its acceleration must point along the
slip. A contact that is *already* sliding has its friction fixed by the sign
of $v_t$, and a negative $a_t$ is the deceleration we want, not a
contradiction. For moving contacts a class is impossible only through its
forces. Applying the starting conditions to a moving contact excludes it for
decelerating, which is the wrong conclusion.

## 9. What an independent check found

A script written from this derivation alone
(`cmg/scripts/checks/class_solve_check.py`, branch `docs/class-solve`)
recomputes $W$, $a_f$ and the class solutions (P, P, P), (P, P, S) and
(P, P, N) at 20 random states of the rest certificate's set, and the pivot's
$W$ and $a_f$ with the velocity terms at tilt rates up to 1 rad/s. The code
agrees to rounding: the largest relative difference is $9\times10^{-15}$.

Two modelling points came out of it.

- **The platform corner's frame.** The code gives both supports the
  platform's frame. The exact frame at the corner is the block face's,
  turned by the tilt offset ($\le 1.08\times10^{-3}$ rad); the supports'
  accelerations differ by at most $7\times10^{-3}$ m/s², about 1%.
- **The disk's slip direction.** The landing hands off a disk that slides
  *up* the face, which is class N in the code's frame, while the rest
  certificate follows class P (sliding down). In P the block decelerates
  at about 0.88 m/s², in N at about 0.72 m/s² (the worked example's numbers).
  This is open and recorded in the technical report, Chapter 19.

## What to remember

- Each contact is **two rows** of a Jacobian; forces enter through the
  **transpose**.
- Eliminating the accelerations gives **$a = W\lambda + a_f$**: $W = JM^{-1}J^\top$
  couples the contacts, $a_f$ holds gravity, the motor and the velocity terms.
- A **class** fixes each contact's state; it makes the problem a square
  linear system, whose solution is checked against the class's conditions.
- On the **flat family** the block does not turn, so there are **no velocity
  terms**: one solve per class serves every speed.
- The **mean-value form** encloses a class solution over a box; a finite
  Jacobian enclosure also proves the system is nonsingular there.
- **Starting and moving differ**: a moving contact may decelerate; only its
  forces can rule its class out.

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- Moreau [@moreau1988unilateral]: the contact problem at the acceleration and velocity levels, the measure-differential formulation behind time stepping.
- Pfeiffer and Glocker [@pfeiffer1996multibody]: multibody systems with unilateral contacts, the classes of contact states and their complementarity formulation, worked engineering examples.
- Brogliato, *Nonsmooth Mechanics* [@brogliato2016nonsmooth]: the standard reference for the Delassus operator, impacts and complementarity systems.
- Pang and Trinkle [@pang1996complementarity]: the acceleration-level problem with Coulomb friction as an LCP, and when solutions exist.
- Stewart and Trinkle [@stewart1996implicit] and Anitescu and Potra [@anitescu1997formulating]: the velocity-level time step, the kind of step map the impact window certifies.
- Neumaier [@neumaier1990interval] and Moore, Kearfott and Cloud [@moore2009introduction]: mean-value forms and interval linear systems.
